connector: Chapter 18 ended with almost eight hundred people aboard the “Lincoln boats.” In Chapter 19 the war really ends. As you read, sort the details: some show the victory is real, and some show it is not finished yet.

a.raw: harriet traveled to washington in february of 1865
a.why: Capital H on Harriet; capital W on Washington (a city); capital F on February (a month); a period ends it. To Washington, in February, and of 1865 are prepositional phrases.

b.raw: three passengers dragged harriet down the aisle into the baggage car
b.fixed: Three passengers dragged Harriet down the aisle into the baggage car.
b.why: Capital T starts the sentence; capital H on Harriet; a period ends it. Down the aisle and into the baggage car are prepositional phrases that tell where.

notes.wordParts: vict = conquer, liber = free, port = carry, matr = mother: victory, liberty, transport, matron.
notes.grammar: A prepositional phrase starts with a preposition (in, on, at, through, past, toward) and ends with a noun. It tells where, when, or how. Find the first word, then the noun that closes the phrase.
notes.spelling: Four suffix rules, one year: double the last consonant after a short vowel (run → running), drop the silent e (hope → hoping), and change y to i (happy → happiest, carry → carried). Look at the end of the base word first.

transcripts.welcome: Hey, it’s Marcus. Chapter 19 is called Victory, and the war really does end. But Sterling doesn’t stop at the celebration. Today’s question: what does victory really mean, and who gets to have it?
transcripts.read: Sort your details into two piles as you read: the victory is real, and the victory isn’t finished. Watch Harriet talk with her parents about pay, a hospital that needs cleaning, and a night in Washington the whole country remembers. Then read the train ride slowly. Decide which pile it goes in.
transcripts.grammar: A prepositional phrase is a little package. It starts with a word like in, on, under, or through, and it ends with a noun. In the baggage car. Through the woods. Find the first word, then find the noun that closes the package.

virtue.title: Real victory, or not yet?
virtue.intro: In Chapter 19 the war ends, but not every moment feels like winning. Read each one. Tap A real victory or Not finished yet.

items.t: Secretary Seward tells her, “This is your victory, Harriet. You fought for it long before the rest of us did.”
items.why: Someone powerful says out loud what Harriet has done.

items.t: Black soldiers are first offered seven dollars a month. White soldiers get thirteen.
items.why: Unequal pay means the fight for fair treatment isn’t over.

items.t: Congress passes a law giving Black soldiers the same pay as white soldiers, even for the months they fought without wages.
items.why: The soldiers who refused unequal pay finally win.

items.t: Charleston falls, and Lee surrenders at Appomattox.
items.why: The Union wins the war that ended slavery.

items.t: Three passengers throw Harriet into the baggage car, even with her War Department pass.
items.why: The war is won, but Black Americans are still not treated as equals.
